Choosing the spending function and the graph together

Source: vignettes/articles/gsd-joint-spending.Rmd
gsd-joint-spending.Rmd

What this article covers

A group sequential design (GSD) looks at the data more than once. Each hypothesis then needs a spending function, which decides how much of its significance level may be used at each look. Spending functions are usually picked from a short list before the graph is optimised. This article shows how multigrain can choose one spending parameter together with the graph, and how to read the result.

It builds on two other articles, which it does not repeat:

  • Getting started explains graphical multiple testing procedures (hypothesis weights 𝐰\mathbf{w} and transition matrix 𝐆\mathbf{G}), gain functions and graph_optimise().
  • Trial success measures explains the group sequential workflow with fixed spending functions: simulate_pvalues_gsd(), transform_pvalues_gsd(), gains that depend on when a hypothesis is rejected (trial_success_gsd() and its discount tables), stopping rules (stopping_rule_gsd()) and graph_optimise_gsd().

The optimisation framework is described in Spiers et al. (2026), Gain-function optimisation of graphical multiple testing procedures for confirmatory clinical trials (arXiv:2609.19994v1). The second example below extends its Example 5.

A short primer on interim analyses and spending

Interim analyses. In a GSD the data are analysed at planned looks, for example once when half the patients have their outcome and once at the end. The amount of data at a look is its information fraction tt: t=0.5t = 0.5 at the halfway look and t=1t = 1 at the final one. If a hypothesis is rejected at an interim look, the trial can stop early for efficacy.

Spending functions. Testing the same hypothesis at full level α\alpha at every look would inflate the type I error. Instead, each hypothesis gets an α-spending function α(t)\alpha(t): the cumulative part of its level that may be used by information fraction tt, rising to the whole level at t=1t = 1. The boundary at each look is set so that the probability of crossing any boundary by that look, under the null hypothesis, equals α(t)\alpha(t). A spending function that spends little early keeps almost the full level for the final analysis; one that spends a lot early makes early rejection more likely but leaves a stricter final boundary.

The Hwang–Shih–DeCani family. The HSD spending functions (gsDesign::sfHSD()) have one parameter γ\gamma:

α(t)=α1−e−γt1−e−γ,γ≠0, \alpha(t) = \alpha \, \frac{1 - e^{-\gamma t}}{1 - e^{-\gamma}}, \qquad \gamma \neq 0,

and α(t)=αt\alpha(t) = \alpha t for γ=0\gamma = 0. Some texts write the parameter as θ\theta. Negative values spend little early: at t=0.5t = 0.5, γ=−4\gamma = -4 has spent about 12% of the level, close to O’Brien–Fleming spending. γ=0\gamma = 0 spends in proportion to information, and γ=1\gamma = 1 has spent about 62% at t=0.5t = 0.5, close to Pocock spending. So one number moves the design smoothly between the two textbook choices.

alpha <- 0.025
t <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
gammas <- c(-4, -2, 0, 1)

spent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gammas, function(g) {
    data.frame(
        t = t,
        spent = gsDesign::sfHSD(alpha, t, g)$spend / alpha,
        curve = sprintf("HSD, gamma = %g", g)
    )
}))
spent <- rbind(
    spent,
    data.frame(
        t = t,
        spent = gsDesign::sfLDOF(alpha, t)$spend / alpha,
        curve = "sfLDOF (O'Brien-Fleming type)"
    )
)
spent$curve <- factor(spent$curve, levels = unique(spent$curve))

ggplot(spent, aes(t, spent, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(rep("solid", 4), "dashed")) +
    labs(
        x = "Information fraction t",
        y = "Proportion of the level spent",
        colour = NULL,
        linetype = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

The dotted line marks the interim look used below. The dashed curve, gsDesign::sfLDOF, is the Lan–DeMets O’Brien–Fleming-type function used for the primary hypothesis throughout.

Why spending and graph should be chosen together

Take two hypotheses: a primary H1H_1 and a key secondary H2H_2, each tested at an interim look (t=0.5t = 0.5) and a final look (t=1t = 1), at one-sided α=0.025\alpha = 0.025. The nominal powers are 0.90 and 0.80 and the test statistics are correlated with ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5. H1H_1 uses gsDesign::sfLDOF.

The gain values H1H_1 at 0.6 and H2H_2 at 0.4. A claim at the final analysis is worth 0.8 of the same claim at the interim (the discount table d), and the trial stops as soon as H1H_1 is rejected:

gain <- trial_success_gsd(0.6 * d(t1) + 0.4 * d(t2), d = c(1, 0.8))
rule <- stopping_rule_gsd(r1)

Here t1 and t2 are the looks at which H1H_1 and H2H_2 were rejected (0 if never), and r1 is “H1H_1 has been rejected”; see Trial success measures for the syntax.

The stopping rule is what ties the spending of H2H_2 to the graph. If H1H_1 is rejected at the interim, the trial stops there, so H2H_2 gets its interim look and nothing else. Whether H2H_2 is rejected in that trial then depends on two things:

  1. How much level the graph gives H2H_2: its own weight w2w_2, plus what H1H_1 passes on once it is rejected.
  2. How much of that level H2H_2’s spending function lets it use at t=0.5t = 0.5. Under O’Brien–Fleming-type spending it is very little.

The graph also decides how often the trial stops: a larger w1w_1 makes an interim rejection of H1H_1, and therefore a stop, more likely. With O’Brien–Fleming-type spending on H2H_2 a stop is costly, so the best graph keeps w1w_1 low. With spending that uses more of the level early, a stop costs less and the best graph can put more weight on H1H_1. The best graph depends on the spending function, and the best spending function depends on the graph, so the two should be chosen together.

Simulate the p-values once

simulate_pvalues_gsd() draws raw p-values at every look; the information fractions are stored with them.

set.seed(20261007)
raw <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(H1 = 0.90, H2 = 0.80),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = c(0.5, 1),
    nsim = 1e5
)

Both runs below use these same draws, so their gains can be compared directly.

Baseline: fixed spending

First, the usual approach: fix the spending of both hypotheses at gsDesign::sfLDOF and optimise the graph alone.

pv_ldof <- transform_pvalues_gsd(raw, spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF)

main_base <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    pv_ldof,
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain,
    stopping_rule = rule
)
main_base
#> <multigrain_graph_optimal>
#> Optimal graph found (given user-defined constraints on graph and computational resources):
#> 
#> Hypothesis weights:
#>     H1     H2 
#> 0.2927 0.7073 
#> 
#> Transition matrix:
#>    H1 H2
#> H1  0  1
#> H2  1  0
#> 
#> Trial success function:
#> 0.6 * d(t1) + 0.4 * d(t2)
#>

Joint optimisation

To let the spending of H2H_2 be chosen, tag it with sf_hsd_opt() in the list of spending functions. transform_pvalues_gsd() then returns a spending spec instead of transformed p-values:

spec <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
spec
#> <multigrain_pvals_gsd_spec>
#> 100000 simulation(s), 2 hypothes(es), 2 analys(es); alpha = 0.025
#> Information fractions (NA = no data at that analysis):
#>    analysis 1 analysis 2
#> H1        0.5          1
#> H2        0.5          1
#> Look-back: H1 = FALSE, H2 = FALSE
#> Spending:
#> H1: gsDesign::sfLDOF
#> H2: sfHSD(param = gamma in [-4, 1])
#> Spending parameters:
#> gamma: bounds [-4, 1], step 0.25, 21 nodes, start -1.5
#> Boundary tables built: 21

The search does not try every real value of γ\gamma. It tries a lattice: by default −4-4 to 11 in steps of 0.250.25, 21 values (sf_hsd_opt() takes bounds and step to change it). For each value the spec holds a boundary table, built and checked when the spec is created; building them is the slow step, about 20 seconds here. The same spec can be reused with other gains and stopping rules on the same draws.

Pass the spec to graph_optimise_gsd() in place of the p-values:

main_joint <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    spec,
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain,
    stopping_rule = rule
)
main_joint
#> <multigrain_graph_optimal>
#> Optimal graph found (given user-defined constraints on graph and computational resources):
#> 
#> Hypothesis weights:
#>     H1     H2 
#> 0.4439 0.5561 
#> 
#> Transition matrix:
#>    H1 H2
#> H1  0  1
#> H2  1  0
#> 
#> Trial success function:
#> 0.6 * d(t1) + 0.4 * d(t2)
#> 
#> Spending functions:
#>   H1: gsDesign::sfLDOF
#>   H2: sfHSD(param = -0.25)   [optimised: gamma, bounds -4 to 1, step 0.25]
#> Gain profile in gamma (graph re-optimised at each value):
#>   within 5e-4 of the maximum on [-0.75, 0]; fixed-graph plateau [-0.75, 0]
#> 
#> Stopping rule:
#> Every interim: r1
#> Hypotheses referenced: up to r1
#> 
#> Value of trial success measure:
#> 0.693

The search runs in two stages. A genetic algorithm first searches the graph and γ\gamma together. Then, at every lattice value of γ\gamma, the graph is re-optimised, starting from a neighbouring value’s graph. The second stage gives the profile: the best achievable gain at each γ\gamma. The chosen value is in main_joint$spending_param and the profile in main_joint$spending_profile.

Comparing the two designs

Design H2 spending w1 w2 g12 g21 Power H1 Power H2 H2 at interim Mean stop look Gain
Fixed spending sfLDOF 0.293 0.707 1 1 0.852 0.739 0.126 1.875 0.6709
Joint sfHSD(param = -0.25) 0.444 0.556 1 1 0.863 0.721 0.319 1.812 0.6930

w1, w2 are the hypothesis weights and g12, g21 the transition weights (H1→H2H_1 \to H_2 and H2→H1H_2 \to H_1). Power H1 and Power H2 are the probabilities of rejecting each hypothesis at any look, H2 at interim the probability of rejecting H2H_2 at the interim, and Mean stop look the average look at which the trial ends.

gridExtra::grid.arrange(
    plot(main_base, title = "Fixed spending (sfLDOF)"),
    plot(main_joint, title = "Joint (sfHSD for H2)"),
    ncol = 2
)

The optimiser chooses γ*=−0.25\gamma^* = -0.25 for H2H_2, which spends much earlier than O’Brien–Fleming, and the gain rises from 0.6709 to 0.6930. The graph moves too: the weight on H1H_1 goes from 0.293 to 0.444. Because H2H_2 can now use more of its level at the interim, a stop after an interim rejection of H1H_1 costs less, so the graph can afford to back the primary hypothesis more.

The overall power of H2H_2 falls slightly, from 0.739 to 0.721, because spending more early leaves a stricter final boundary. But H2H_2 is now rejected at the interim in 0.319 of trials instead of 0.126, and under this gain and stopping rule an earlier claim is worth more than a slightly likelier late one.

Reading the output

The spending lines in print(). Under Spending functions: each hypothesis has a label. A tagged hypothesis shows the chosen function, here sfHSD(param = -0.25), marked [optimised: ...] with the parameter’s name (gamma, or the id given to sf_hsd_opt()), its bounds and its step. The next lines sum up the profile as two plateaus, explained below.

The profile table in summary(). summary() prints the graph, the gain, the power and the constraints, followed by the profile, which is shown here:

summary(main_joint)
#> Spending-parameter profile (gamma):
#>  value   gain gain_fixed_graph   diff      se n_eval

#>  -3.00 0.6852           0.6852 0.0078 0.00028     26
#>  -2.75 0.6864           0.6864 0.0066 0.00028     26
#>  -2.50 0.6876           0.6875 0.0055 0.00027     26
#>  -2.25 0.6886           0.6885 0.0045 0.00026     26
#>  -2.00 0.6896           0.6896 0.0034 0.00026     28
#>  -1.75 0.6906           0.6905 0.0024 0.00024     24
#>  -1.50 0.6913           0.6913 0.0017 0.00023     24
#>  -1.25 0.6918           0.6918 0.0012 0.00020     28
#>  -1.00 0.6923           0.6923 0.0007 0.00018     29

#>  -0.50 0.6929           0.6929 0.0001 0.00012     34
#>  -0.25 0.6930           0.6930 0.0000 0.00000     26
#>   0.00 0.6928           0.6927 0.0003 0.00014     25
#>   0.25 0.6925           0.6924 0.0005 0.00015     27
#>   0.50 0.6921           0.6920 0.0009 0.00018     26
#>   0.75 0.6914           0.6913 0.0016 0.00022     28
#>   1.00 0.6906           0.6905 0.0024 0.00026     25
#> GA visited 21 of 21 nodes

Each row is one lattice value of γ\gamma:

  • gain: the best gain at that value, with the graph re-optimised there.
  • gain_fixed_graph: the gain at that value of the graph chosen overall, kept as it is.
  • diff: how far gain falls short of the optimum. Every row is computed on the same simulated trials, so the difference is paired and much more precise than either gain on its own.
  • se: the standard error of diff. It is 0 at the chosen value.
  • n_eval: the number of gain evaluations the local search used at that value.

Plateaus. A plateau is the run of γ\gamma values around the optimum whose gain is within 5×10−45 \times 10^{-4} of the best. Inside it the differences are a few standard errors at most, so the values are as good as each other for practical purposes. print() reports two: one for gain (graph re-optimised at each γ\gamma) and one for gain_fixed_graph (graph held at the chosen one). The plot below draws the value, gain and gain_fixed_graph columns of main_joint$spending_profile:

The shaded band is the plateau of gain; the dotted line marks γ*\gamma^*.

How to use the plateau when writing a protocol:

  • A wide plateau means the gain hardly depends on γ\gamma within that range. Pick a round, easily justified value inside it and pre-specify it; nothing is lost by not using γ*\gamma^* exactly.
  • A narrow plateau means γ\gamma matters. Report the chosen value with the graph, and check it on fresh simulations (next section).
  • The fixed-graph plateau narrower than the re-optimised one means the best graph changes with γ\gamma. If you move γ\gamma within the wider plateau, re-optimise the graph at the new value too.
  • An optimum on a bound of the lattice means the gain may still rise beyond it. Widen bounds in sf_hsd_opt() (from −10-10 up to 22) and run again.

In this design both plateaus run from −0.75-0.75 to 00. Any γ\gamma in that range is as good as γ*\gamma^* to within the simulation error, and since the two plateaus agree, the best graph barely moves across it. At γ=−4\gamma = -4, close to O’Brien–Fleming, the gain is 0.0128 lower, about 39 standard errors.

Checking the chosen design on fresh simulations

The graph and γ\gamma were chosen on the same simulated trials that score them, so the reported gain is slightly optimistic (the “winner’s curse”). To check it, simulate new p-values, build a spec from them with the same spending functions, and use resolve_pvalues_gsd() to obtain the transformed p-values at the chosen γ\gamma. Then evaluate the chosen graph on them:

set.seed(20261008)
raw_new <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(H1 = 0.90, H2 = 0.80),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = c(0.5, 1),
    nsim = 1e5
)
spec_new <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw_new,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
pv_new <- resolve_pvalues_gsd(spec_new, main_joint$spending_param)

check <- calc_power_pvals_gsd(
    pv_new,
    hyp_weight = main_joint$hyp_weight,
    trans_matrix = main_joint$trans_matrix,
    stopping_rule = rule,
    custom_power = list(gain = gain)
)
round(check$gain, 4)
#> [1] 0.6936

On fresh draws the design scores 0.6936, against 0.6930 reported by the optimiser. Only lattice values can be resolved, because only their boundary tables were built and checked.

A second example: the paper’s Example 5

Example 5 of the paper has two endpoints with different timing. Progression-free survival (PFS, H1H_1) is complete at the interim analysis: its information fraction is 1 at both looks, so its spending function has no effect. Overall survival (OS, H2H_2) has 70% of its information at the interim and all of it at the final analysis. The nominal powers are 0.98 and 0.93 and ρ=0.5\rho = 0.5. PFS is valued at 0.4 and OS at 0.6. A PFS claim made only at the final analysis keeps half its value, and an OS claim at the final analysis keeps 75%. There is no stopping rule.

The paper fixes O’Brien–Fleming-type spending for OS. Here we let OS’s spending be chosen with the graph:

set.seed(20261014)
raw5 <- simulate_pvalues_gsd(
    power_nominal = c(PFS = 0.98, OS = 0.93),
    corr_matrix = matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 1), nrow = 2),
    info_frac = rbind(PFS = c(1, 1), OS = c(0.7, 1)),
    nsim = 1e5
)
gain5 <- trial_success_gsd(
    0.4 * d_pfs(t1) + 0.6 * d_os(t2),
    d_pfs = c(1, 0.50),
    d_os = c(1, 0.75)
)

# baseline: OS spending fixed at sfLDOF
ex5_base <- graph_optimise_gsd(
    transform_pvalues_gsd(raw5, spending = gsDesign::sfLDOF),
    graph_constraint_free(2),
    gain5
)

# joint: OS tagged
spec5 <- transform_pvalues_gsd(
    raw5,
    spending = list(gsDesign::sfLDOF, sf_hsd_opt())
)
ex5_joint <- graph_optimise_gsd(spec5, graph_constraint_free(2), gain5)
ex5_joint
#> <multigrain_graph_optimal>
#> Optimal graph found (given user-defined constraints on graph and computational resources):
#> 
#> Hypothesis weights:
#>     H1     H2 
#> 0.8596 0.1404 
#> 
#> Transition matrix:
#>    H1 H2
#> H1  0  1
#> H2  1  0
#> 
#> Trial success function:
#> 0.4 * d_pfs(t1) + 0.6 * d_os(t2)
#> 
#> Spending functions:
#>   H1: gsDesign::sfLDOF
#>   H2: sfHSD(param = -0.5)   [optimised: gamma, bounds -4 to 1, step 0.25]
#> Gain profile in gamma (graph re-optimised at each value):
#>   within 5e-4 of the maximum on [-1.25, 0.25]; fixed-graph plateau [-1.25, 0.25]
#> 
#> Value of trial success measure:
#> 0.9127
Design OS spending w PFS w OS Power PFS Power OS OS at interim Gain
Fixed spending sfLDOF 0.87 0.13 0.978 0.919 0.663 0.9038
Joint sfHSD(param = -0.5) 0.86 0.14 0.977 0.906 0.761 0.9127

OS at interim is the proportion of trials in which OS is rejected at the interim analysis.

Even without a stopping rule, the time discount rewards spending earlier for OS. The optimiser chooses γ*=−0.5\gamma^* = -0.5, OS is rejected at the interim in 0.761 of trials instead of 0.663, and the gain rises from 0.9038 to 0.9127.

This example differs from the first in two ways:

  • The graph hardly moves. The weight on PFS goes from 0.870 to 0.860, and the two plateaus are the same. Without a stopping rule an interim rejection of PFS costs OS nothing, so the coupling between the graph and the spending is weak. Here the spending could have been chosen on its own.
  • The plateau is wide, from −1.25-1.25 to 0.250.25. Any value in that range, including the conventional γ=0\gamma = 0 (spending in proportion to information), would do. Both textbook ends are clearly worse, O’Brien–Fleming-like spending much more so than Pocock-like spending.

Simulation error does not affect error control

Monte Carlo error and the coarseness of the lattice affect only the power and gain reported for a design, never its familywise error rate: every value of γ\gamma the search can choose has a boundary table checked before the search starts, and the procedure controls the error rate for any fixed choice.
